title: Requirements
subtitle: The cheapest bug to fix is the one caught before any code: get the right thing specified.

sections.title: Functional and non-functional
sections.body: Functional requirements say what the system does (“a user can reset a password by email”). Non-functional requirements constrain how: performance, security, usability, availability, portability. A good requirement is testable: “responds in under 2 s for 95 % of requests” not “fast”.

questions.prompt: “The site must handle 1000 users at once” is…

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It constrains quality, not a feature.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: It states a need, not a solution.

sections.title: Eliciting requirements
sections.body: Techniques: interviews, questionnaires, observation, workshops, prototypes, studying existing documents. Stakeholders disagree; requirements must be negotiated and prioritised (e.g. MoSCoW: must, should, could, won’t).

sections.title: Use cases and user stories
sections.body: A use case describes an actor achieving a goal in steps, with alternate flows for failures. A user story: “As a role I want goal so that benefit”, with acceptance criteria. Stories are small and estimated in points.

sections.title: The SRS
sections.body: A Software Requirements Specification (IEEE 830/29148) contains: introduction (purpose, scope, definitions), overall description (users, constraints), specific requirements (functional, external interfaces, performance, design constraints), and appendices. It must be complete, consistent, unambiguous, verifiable and traceable.

sections.title: Validation and change
sections.body: Validate by reviews, prototypes and test-case writing. Requirements change; manage change with a recorded process: request → impact analysis → approval → update and trace. Traceability links each requirement to design, code and tests.

worked.why: A project has 120 requirements; 24 change after baseline.

choices.text: An iterative process and strict change control.

sections.title: Sizing from requirements: function points
sections.body: Function points count user-visible functions: external inputs (EI), outputs (EO), inquiries (EQ), internal files (ILF), external interfaces (EIF), each weighted by complexity. Unadjusted FP = Σ count × weight; multiply by a value adjustment factor (0.65–1.35).

worked.why: Average weights: EI 4, EO 5, EQ 4, ILF 10, EIF 7. Counts: EI 10, EO 6, EQ 5, ILF 4, EIF 2.

questions.prompt: Function points are useful because they are…

responses.title: A tempting idea.
responses.body: They can be counted from requirements.
